title: San Jacinto Club, Lions Club and his grandfather
summary: The interviewer recalls recording at the San Jacinto in 1944; Justin describes the rival Lions Club, later a funeral parlor run by his grandfather.

story.theme_name: Dance halls, lake camps and riverboat bandstands
story.community_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played

blocks.x: I recorded there. I recorded George Lewis and Buck Johnson. Oh did you? Yes, in 1944. I recorded there one whole week, six nights. Oh, that used to be quite a spot.
Well do you remember the old Lions Club which is located about three blocks from there? No. Near Claiborne Street.
Oh yes, that was quite a spot too.
There's a carnival club, a white carnival club uptown they call Lions Club uptown.

No, this was a club, it was on the same basis as San Jacinto's Club. And I think the club I always thought was in competition with San Jacinto's Club. And they used to always try to outdo one another by having various bands and of course at that time they used to call them Buck Dancers and of course we'd call them Sessions now and see which had the best group and whatnot. But as of now it's been converted to a funeral parlor now. Oh I think I know. So that's why you probably haven't paid any attention to it and I think it was converted way back, as far back as 1933. Well I know. 33 or 34. I have a picture of a funeral, a brass band, right in front of it and I know where it is.
Yeah, well of course at that time my grandfather was president of the club.

As a matter of fact he himself turned into a funeral parlor. And because he had his place out there on St. Philip Street between Murray and Liberty. What's his name? Raul J. Lopes. He was the Lopes of the coin, the Lopes establishment on St. Philip Street.
Yeah I remember another funeral parlor on St. Philip too.
